summary: Describes how to provide call transfer in SIP using extensions such as REFER and Replaces, covering blind, consultative and attended transfer. It is part of the SIP multiparty call control framework, and is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This document describes how a SIP phone hands an ongoing call to a third party. The party making the transfer names the new party, the party being transferred places a new call to them, and the result is reported back so that a failed transfer can be undone.

subtitle: How SIP endpoints hand a call to someone else, using REFER and Replaces, from blind to attended transfer.

tldr.problem: SIP itself has no way to move an established call to a third party, and the ways to do it in practice differ in whether the parties can see each other and whether a failed transfer can be undone.
tldr.mechanism: The Transferor sends a REFER to the Transferee naming the Transfer Target, and the Transferee places a new call to that target and reports the outcome back with NOTIFY. The Replaces header field lets the target take over the call that the transferor had with the transferee.
tldr.outcome: The document gives a Best Current Practice for basic, consultative and attended transfer, including how to recover when a transfer fails and how to protect the target's address from the party being transferred.

sections.title: What the Document Covers
sections.content:
The document describes providing call transfer capabilities and requirements in SIP, as defined in RFC 3261. The work is part of the multiparty call control framework.

The mechanisms discussed are most closely related to traditional basic and consultation hold transfers. It details the use of the REFER method of RFC 3515 and the Replaces header field of RFC 3891 to achieve the transfer. A user agent that fully supports the mechanisms described supports REFER and Replaces in addition to RFC 3261, should use a Contact URI that meets the requirements in Section 8.1.1.8 of RFC 3261, and supports the Target-Dialog header field of RFC 4538.

The document does not prescribe the flows precisely as they are shown. The flows illustrate the principles of best practice for the transfer feature, and they are well-reviewed examples of SIP usage that implement transfer with REFER, which are Best Common Practice according to IETF consensus. In most of the examples the Transferor is in the atlanta.example.com domain, the Transferee is in biloxi.example.com and the Transfer Target is in chicago.example.com.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives worked examples of transferring a call, showing the messages each party sends. The examples are there to show the principles rather than to fix an exact sequence, and they are marked as good practice agreed by the IETF.

sections.title: Actors and Roles
sections.content:
There are three actors in a given transfer event, each playing one of three roles. The Transferee is the party being transferred to the Transfer Target. The Transferor is the party initiating the transfer. The Transfer Target is the new party being introduced into a call with the Transferee.

Three further roles are used to describe transfer requirements and scenarios. The Originator wishes to place a call to the Recipient and is the source of the first INVITE in a session, to either a Facilitator or a Screener. The Facilitator receives a call or an out-of-band request from the Originator, establishes a call to the Recipient through the Screener, and connects the Originator to the Recipient; it typically acts on behalf of the Originator. The Screener receives a call ultimately intended for the Recipient and transfers the calling party to the Recipient if appropriate; it typically acts on behalf of the Recipient. The Recipient is the party to which the Originator is ultimately connected.
sections.plainLanguage: A transfer has three parties: the one who hands the call over, the one whose call is handed over, and the new party who receives it. The document also names three roles used in the examples, where an originator asks a facilitator to reach a recipient through a screener.

sections.title: The Six Requirements
sections.content:
The document lists six requirements for call transfer.

  1. Any party in a SIP session must be able to transfer any other party in that session at any point in that session.
  2. The Transferor and the Transferee must not be removed from a session as part of a transfer transaction. The RFC notes that at first glance this may seem to indicate that the user experience in a transfer must be significantly different from what a current PBX or Centrex user expects, but as the call flows show this is not the case, and a client may preserve the current experience. Without this requirement, some forms of the current experience, such as ringback on transfer failure, would be lost.
  3. The Transferor must know whether or not the transfer was successful.
  4. The Transferee must be able to replace an existing dialog with a new dialog.
  5. The Transferor and Transferee should indicate their support for the primitives required to achieve transfer.
  6. The Transferor should provide the Transfer Target and Transferee with information about the nature and progress of the transfer operation being attempted. To meet this requirement, the transfer operation can be modelled as an ad hoc conference between three parties, as described in Section 9.
sections.plainLanguage: Six requirements shape the design. Any party can hand over any other party at any time, the two of them stay in the session so that a failure can be undone, the person handing over learns whether it worked, and the party handed over can swap its existing call for a new one.

sections.title: Using REFER to Achieve Call Transfer
sections.content:
A REFER can be issued by the Transferor to cause the Transferee to issue an INVITE to the Transfer Target. A successful REFER transaction does not terminate the session between the Transferor and the Transferee; if those parties wish to terminate it they must do so with a subsequent BYE request. The media negotiated between the Transferee and the Transfer Target is not affected by the media negotiated between the Transferor and the Transferee. The INVITE issued by the Transferee carries the same Session Description Protocol body it would have if the Transferee had initiated that INVITE on its own, and the disposition of the media streams between the Transferor and the Transferee is not altered by the REFER method. Agents may alter a session's media through additional signalling, for example the SIP hold re-INVITE of RFC 3261 or the conferencing extensions.

The Transferor and Transferee could reuse the existing dialog to send the REFER, which would result in a single dialog shared by two uses, an invite usage and a subscription usage. The approach in this document avoids dialog reuse, because of the difficulties described in RFC 5057. Three motivations for reusing the dialog are listed: there was no way to ensure that a REFER on a new dialog would reach the particular endpoint involved in a transfer, since implementation details and changes in proxy routing between an INVITE and a REFER could send the REFER to the wrong place; it was unclear how to associate an existing invite usage with a REFER arriving on a new dialog; and there were concerns about authorising out-of-dialog REFERs, because the authorisation policy for REFER in most implementations piggybacks on the authorisation policy for INVITE.

Globally Routable UA URIs address the first problem, and the Target-Dialog header field addresses the second, which also lets the existing REFER authorisation policy be reused. As a result, if the Transferee supports the target-dialog extension and the Transferor knows the Contact URI is routable outside the dialog, the REFER should be sent in a new dialog. If the nature of the Contact URI is not known, or if support for the target-dialog extension is not known, the REFER should be sent inside the existing dialog. A Transferee must be prepared to receive a REFER either inside or outside a dialog. A Transferor can know that a Contact URI is routable outside a dialog by validation, for example sending an OPTIONS and receiving a response, or if it satisfies the properties described in the GRUU specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The transfer works by one party sending a REFER that names the new party. The party being transferred then makes its own call, so the media is negotiated fresh and the original call is not torn down. The REFER is normally sent outside the original call, and the Target-Dialog header field ties it back to that call.

sections.title: Basic Transfer and Failure Recovery
sections.content:
Basic transfer consists of the Transferor providing the Transfer Target's contact to the Transferee. The Transferee attempts to establish a session using that contact and reports the results of the attempt to the Transferor. The signalling relationship between the Transferor and Transferee is not terminated, so the call is recoverable if the Transfer Target cannot be reached. The Transfer Target's contact information has been exposed to the Transferee, and the provided contact can be used to make new calls in the future.

The participants in a basic transfer should indicate support for the REFER and NOTIFY methods in Allow header fields in INVITE, 200 OK to INVITE and OPTIONS messages, and should also indicate support for Target-Dialog in the Supported header field. In the flows the dialog between the Transferor and the Transferee stays connected, on hold, during the REFER process, which gives the greatest flexibility for recovery from failure. If the Transferor's agent does not wish to take part in the rest of the REFER process and has no intention of assisting with recovery from transfer failure, it could send a BYE to the Transferee as soon as the REFER transaction completes; that flow is sometimes known as unattended transfer or blind transfer.

Figure 1 shows a transfer where the Transferee uses a GRUU, supports the target-dialog extension and says so, so the Transferor sends the REFER outside the INVITE dialog and the Transferee matches it to the existing dialog with the Target-Dialog header field. The Transferor receives 202 Accepted, then a NOTIFY carrying 100 Trying, then the Transferee places the INVITE to the Transfer Target, and finally a NOTIFY carrying 200 OK reports the outcome before the Transferor sends the BYE.

Two failure cases are shown. When the Transfer Target is busy, the Transferee's INVITE is answered with 486 Busy Here, and the Transferor is told of that through a NOTIFY, after which it takes the Transferee off hold and resumes the session. When the Transfer Target does not answer, the Transferee gives up waiting, sends a CANCEL, and the INVITE is answered with 487 Request Cancelled, which is reported to the Transferor in the same way. After a transfer failure the Transferor takes the Transferee off hold and resumes the session.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic transfer is: hand over the new party's address, let the party being transferred call them, and report back what happened. If the new party is busy or does not answer, the original call is still there, so it is simply resumed.

sections.title: Consultation Hold and Attended Transfer
sections.content:
Transfer with consultation hold involves a session between the Transferor and the Transfer Target before the transfer actually takes place, and is implemented with SIP Hold and the transfer described above. A useful feature is to let the target know that the session relates to an intended transfer: since many user agents render the display name in the From header field to the user, a consultation INVITE could contain a string such as Incoming consultation from Transferor with intent to transfer Transferee.

Exposing the transfer target means the Transferor places the Transferee on hold, establishes a call with the Transfer Target to alert them to the impending transfer, terminates that connection and then proceeds with the transfer. This variation gives an experience similar to that expected by current PBX and Centrex users. Protecting the transfer target reverses the roles: the Transferor places the Transferee on hold, establishes a call with the Transfer Target and then transfers the original Transfer Target to the original Transferee. That hides information about the original Transfer Target from the original Transferee, but the Transferee's experience differs from current systems, because the Transferee is effectively called back by the Transfer Target. A problem with this simplest implementation is that the Transferee receives a new call from the Transfer Target, and unless its agent has a reliable way to associate this new call with the call it already has with the Transferor, it has to alert the new call as a separate call. Without a call-waiting-like user interface, the Transferee might be stuck returning a Busy-Here to the Transfer Target, effectively preventing the transfer. The RFC notes that there are many ways correlation could be provided, for instance by passing the dialog parameters directly as header parameters in the Refer-To URI.

In the attended transfer, the Transferor places the Transferee on hold, establishes a call with the Transfer Target to alert them, places the target on hold, and then proceeds with the transfer using an escaped Replaces header field in the Refer-To header. The Contact URI of the Transfer Target should be used as the Refer-To URI unless the URI is suspected or known not to be routable outside the dialog; otherwise the Address of Record of the Transfer Target should be used, which is the same URI the Transferor used to establish the session. If the triggered INVITE is routed to a different user agent than the Transfer Target, the Require: replaces header field should be used in it, to prevent a user agent that does not support Replaces from ignoring it and answering without a dialog match. If proxy or service routing prevents the triggered INVITE from reaching the same user agent, it fails with a timeout, 403 or 404, and the Transferee may then retry the transfer with the Refer-To URI set to the Contact URI.

The RFC also covers recovery when one party does not support REFER, in which case a transfer with consultation hold can still be completed if the Transferor and one other party support it; a 405 Method Not Allowed might be returned instead of the 501 Not Implemented response. A semi-attended transfer is one where the Transferor ends the attempt to contact the Transfer Target before the session is established but still proceeds with the transfer, for example knowing that the Transferee will end up talking to the Transfer Target's voicemail service. In that flow the Transferor's user agent continues the transfer as an attended transfer even after the Transferor hangs up, and media must be played to the Transfer Target upon answer, or the target may hang up and the transfer will fail. Finally, an attended transfer can fall back to a basic transfer: if the Transfer Target does not support Replaces, the INVITE is rejected with a 420 Bad Extension response and the Transferor switches from attended transfer to basic transfer immediately.
sections.plainLanguage: With a consultation hold, the party handing over calls the new party first, so the new party knows what is coming. The attended variant goes further: the new party takes over the call using the Replaces header, so the person being transferred hears the new party straight away. The document also covers what to do when a party does not support REFER or Replaces.

sections.title: Referred-By, Conferences and Multiple Parties
sections.content:
In the examples so far, the Transfer Target has no definitive information about which party initiated the transfer, or even that a transfer is taking place. The Referred-By mechanism of RFC 3892 gives the Transferor a way to let the Transferee tell the Transfer Target who initiated the transfer. The simplest and least secure approach is to include the Referred-By header field in the REFER, which is then copied into the triggered INVITE. A more secure mechanism involves the Referred-By security token, which is generated and signed by the Transferor and passed in a message body to the Transferee and then to the Transfer Target.

A transfer can also be run as an ad hoc conference. In the flow in Section 9, one party does an attended transfer of another to a third, and to keep both of them fully informed of the nature and state of the operation it acts as a focus and hosts an ad hoc conference involving all three. The two other parties subscribe to the conference package of the focus, which lets them know the exact status of the operation, and the focus deletes the conference once the transfer is complete. This flow meets requirement 6 of Section 4. The RFC notes that any type of semi-attended transfer can be implemented using this model, and that the focus could introduce additional media signals such as simulated ring tone or on-hold announcements to improve the user experience.

Section 10 gives an example with multiple parties, in which an Originator places a call to a Facilitator, who reaches the Recipient through a Screener. The Recipient's contact information is exposed to the Facilitator and the Originator. The RFC says this example is provided for clarification of the semantics of the REFER method only, and that it should not be used as the design of an implementation.

Finally, Section 11 covers gateway transfer issues. A gateway in SIP acts as a user agent, so the whole discussion applies to gateways as well as native endpoints, but there are gateway-specific problems. In a hairpin case, where the Transferee and the Transfer Target both sit on the PSTN side of a gateway, it is often desirable to remove the gateway from the loop, which is only possible if both legs of the target call are on the same gateway. The problem is how to give the proxy enough information to know to route the call to the same gateway: in the consultative case the target INVITE includes the Replaces header, which contains dialog information that can be used to relate it to the consultation, but there is no information that relates the target call to the original one, and in the blind case the target dialog cannot be related to the original dialog either. The RFC also describes a glare-like problem when a consultative transfer turns blind: the Transferor hangs up, the Transfer Target on the gateway answers just after the CANCEL, and the Transferee gets a busy response or the user's voicemail. The recommended behaviour is to use the approach in Section 7.6. The RFC notes that solutions to these gateway-specific issues may involve new extensions to SIP in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The document also covers three extras. The Referred-By header tells the new party who arranged the transfer. Running the transfer as a small conference lets everyone watch its progress. And gateways have their own problems, where the two ends of the new call end up on different gateways and the transfer has to be done twice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The call transfer flows are implemented using the REFER and Replaces call control primitives in SIP, so the security considerations in the REFER and Replaces documents must be followed. The document addresses the issue of protecting the Address of Record URI of a Transfer Target in Sections 7.1 and 7.2.

Any REFER request must be appropriately authenticated and authorised using standard SIP mechanisms, or calls may be hijacked. A user agent may use local policy or human intervention in deciding whether or not to accept a REFER. When generating NOTIFY responses based on the outcome of the triggered request, care should be taken in constructing the message body so that no private information is leaked.

An INVITE containing a Replaces header field should only be accepted if it has been properly authenticated and authorised using standard SIP mechanisms, and the requestor is authorised to perform the dialog replacement. Special care is needed if the replaced dialog uses additional media streams compared to the original dialog, in which case the user must authorise the addition of new media streams in a dialog replacement. The same mechanism used to authorise the addition of a media stream in a re-INVITE could be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The transfer messages carry the same risk as the rest of SIP signalling. A REFER must be authenticated and authorised or calls can be hijacked, and the progress reports sent back must not leak private details. Replacing a call that has extra media streams needs the user's approval.

viz.caption: The six requirements for SIP call transfer

items.title: Any party, any time
items.text: Any party in a session must be able to transfer any other party in that session at any point in it.

items.title: Nobody is dropped
items.text: The Transferor and the Transferee must not be removed from the session as part of the transfer, so a failure can be undone.

items.title: The outcome is known
items.text: The Transferor must know whether or not the transfer was successful.

items.title: The dialog can be replaced
items.text: The Transferee must be able to replace an existing dialog with a new dialog.

items.title: Support is advertised
items.text: The Transferor and Transferee should indicate their support for the primitives needed for the transfer.

items.title: Progress is reported
items.text: The Transferor should give the Transfer Target and the Transferee information about the nature and progress of the transfer.

viz.caption: The security rules the transfer flows must follow

items.title: Authenticate and authorise the REFER
items.text: Any REFER must be appropriately authenticated and authorised using standard SIP mechanisms, or calls may be hijacked.

items.title: Decide whether to accept
items.text: A user agent may use local policy or human intervention in deciding whether to accept a REFER.

items.title: Do not leak private details
items.text: When building the NOTIFY bodies that report the outcome of the triggered request, care is needed so that no private information is leaked.

items.title: Authorise the dialog replacement
items.text: An INVITE carrying a Replaces header should only be accepted when it is properly authenticated and authorised, and the requestor is allowed to replace the dialog.

items.title: Ask the user about new media streams
items.text: If the replaced dialog uses more media streams than the original, the user must authorise the addition, using the same mechanism as for a re-INVITE.
